An owner of residential real property cannot raise the rent on a covered unit by more than 5% plus the local change in the cost of living (CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, and can only impose up to two such increases within that 12-month period. The cap does not apply to the initial rent set for a new tenancy once prior tenants have vacated. Key value: 5% + CPI, max 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California state law requires landlords to give tenants at least 30 days' written advance notice before a rent increase that is less than 10%. Key value: 30 days' notice for increases < 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 827; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a prospective tenant furnishes the landlord with a reusable (portable) tenant screening report, the landlord must use that report rather than requiring the applicant to pay for a new one. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A housing provider may check an applicant's criminal history, but may not rely on arrests that did not lead to conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or juvenile justice records, and may not impose a blanket ban excluding all applicants with any criminal history. Any denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and to the health and safety of others, considering the nature/severity of the offense and time elapsed. [Cal. Code Regs. tit. 2, § 12269; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords may not use a financial or income standard for rental housing that fails to count the combined income of unmarried co-applicants the same way it would count married applicants' combined income. When an applicant has a government rent subsidy, the landlord's income-eligibility standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant personally pays, and if the landlord uses the applicant's credit history, it must let the applicant instead provide alternative proof of ability to pay (e.g., benefit records, pay stubs, bank statements) and reasonably consider that evidence. [Cal. Gov. Code § 12955; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord generally cannot demand or receive a security deposit worth more than one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent. Narrow exceptions allow higher deposits for small landlords, long-term leases, and in certain service-member cases, and deposits must be itemized and returned within 21 days of move-out. Key value: 1 month's rent (up to 2 months' rent for small landlords: natural persons/LLCs of natural persons owning ≤2 rental properties totaling ≤4 units). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords evicting a tenant for an enumerated not-at-fault reason (owner/family/manager occupancy, demolition/conversion/removal from rental use, government order to vacate, HUD-ordered vacation, residential hotel conversion, conversion to affordable housing, or demolition/conversion to condos/hotels/commercial use) from a unit covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or Just Cause Ordinance (JCO) must pay relocation assistance per unit and file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD before serving the termination notice, with a copy of the notice filed with LAHD within 3 days of service. Relocation amounts (effective 7/1/2026-6/30/2027) range from $11,000 (eligible tenant, <3 years) to $27,400 (qualified tenant, 3+ years or low income), paid within 15 days of the notice, and increase every July 1. Key value: $11,000-$27,400 per unit by tenant/tenancy category (Chart A, 7/1/2026-6/30/2027), increasing every July 1; payment due within 15 days of notice. [L.A. Mun. Code § 151.09; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is built after 1978-10-01). Landlords of most residential rental units in the City of Los Angeles that are NOT regulated by the City's Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) may terminate a tenancy only for an enumerated just cause, once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired (whichever comes first). At-fault causes (no relocation assistance owed) include failure to pay rent, uncured lease violations, nuisance or property damage, illegal use of the unit, failure to renew a similar rental agreement, denying the landlord reasonable access, or an unapproved subtenant remaining after the lease ends. No-fault causes (owner/immediate-family move-in, required resident-manager move-in, demolition/permanent removal from the rental market/conversion to non-residential use, government order to vacate, HUD sale of the property, conversion/demolition of a residential hotel, or conversion to affordable housing) require the landlord to pay the tenant relocation assistance. Separately, effective March 27, 2023, a landlord in an RSO or JCO unit may not evict a tenant for unpaid rent unless the amount owed exceeds the HUD Fair Market Rent for the unit's bedroom size. Landlords must register covered units annually with LAHD, display the Registration Certificate, post a Notice of Right to Counsel (beginning August 20, 2025), and provide/post a Notice of Renters' Protections for tenancies beginning or renewing on or after January 27, 2023. All eviction notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days of service. [L.A. Municipal Code § 151.30; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. For 'Protected Units' demolished for new construction, the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict or Notice of Intent to Withdraw with LAHD, serve tenants written notice, and provide occupant protections including the right to relocation, the right to remain in the unit up to 6 months before construction begins (with 6-month move-out notice), the right to return to the unit if demolition does not proceed, a right of first refusal to the new building for some tenants, and tenant notification requirements. Lower-income households must be paid enhanced relocation (Chart B); above-low-income households receive RSO/JCO Chart A amounts. The owner must choose one of three compliance options (standardized payment, comparable replacement unit, or individualized relocation) and pay the highest amount required by State and City law. Key value: Chart B lower-income relocation (7/1/2026-6/30/2027): Extremely Low $115,480; Very Low $96,750; Low Income per Chart A ($14,400 eligible/$27,400 qualified); above-low-income per Chart A ($11,000-$27,400); penalty starting at $250,000 per displaced unit for noncompliance. [L.A. Ord. No. 188481; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is built after 1978-10-01). Landlords of covered rental units in the City of Los Angeles may only terminate a tenancy for a specific list of 'at-fault' or 'no-fault' reasons; tenants evicted for a no-fault reason (e.g., owner/family move-in, demolition, conversion to non-residential use, government order to vacate) are entitled to relocation assistance, while tenants evicted for an at-fault reason (e.g., nonpayment of rent, lease violation, nuisance) are not. Landlords must also register covered units annually, post required tenant-protection and right-to-counsel notices, and file all eviction notices with LAHD within 3 business days of service. For nonpayment-based evictions, a landlord may not evict a tenant whose unpaid rent does not exceed the applicable Fair Market Rent (FMR) for the unit's bedroom size. [Los Angeles Municipal Code ch. XV, art. 1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords of units covered by the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) may raise rent once a year by an annually-announced percentage; for the period July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026 that allowable increase is 3%. Starting February 2, 2026, landlords can no longer tack on an additional percentage increase for utilities on top of the allowable increase. Key value: 3%. [L.A. Mun. Code § 151.06; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0438.explanation: Applies. Landlords, agents, or subcontractors may not pay or contract with a service provider that uses algorithms or software to collect competitor data and recommend rent prices, occupancy levels, or lease terms. Service providers are also banned from facilitating agreements among landlords not to compete on rental pricing or terms. Key value: Fine of $100-$2000 per day for subsequent violations. Possible conflict with P.L.2026, c.43: flagged for human review. [Jersey City, N.J. Code of Ordinances § 218-12; source retrieved 2026-10-03]

Applies (building is at least 5 units, not a single-family home). Jersey City's Rent Control Ordinance (Chapter 260 of the Municipal Code) regulates rent increases for covered rental properties and is administered by the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations and the Rent Leveling Board. Properties with 1 to 4 units are exempt from rent control, so the ordinance's increase limits apply only to buildings of 5 or more units, subject to other permitted exemptions landlords may request. Key value: 1-4 unit properties exempt (rent control applies to 5+ unit buildings). [Jersey City Mun. Code ch. 260; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Enacted but not yet in force: takes effect 2027-07-01. Bans landlords from using, paying for, or facilitating an algorithmic 'coordinator' (software or device) that collects competitively sensitive data (prices, lease terms, security deposits, occupancy levels) from multiple rental property owners to set or recommend rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Also bans two or more rental property owners from engaging in tacit or express 'parallel pricing coordination' on rents, and makes any violation a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act. Possible conflict with Jersey City, N.J. Code of Ordinances § 218-12: flagged for human review. [P.L.2026, c.43; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not a single-family home). A landlord or their agent cannot charge an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental dwelling that exceeds $50. The cap is adjusted annually for inflation (CPI) and published by the Division of Consumer Affairs. Key value: $50 (adjusted annually by CPI). [N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is at least 2 units). Owners of rooming and boarding houses must follow the same good-cause and notice requirements as the general Eviction Law when evicting residents, unless the Department's Bureau of Rooming and Boarding House Standards orders otherwise. [N.J.A.C. 5:27-3.3; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord may evict a residential tenant only for one of the statutory good causes (e.g., nonpayment of rent, disorderly conduct, property damage, substantial lease violation, owner retirement of the property from residential use, conversion to condominium/cooperative, certain criminal convictions on the premises). Except for nonpayment of rent, each cause must be described in a written Notice to Quit (sometimes preceded by a Notice to Cease), with required notice periods ranging from 3 days to 18 months depending on the cause, before an eviction suit may be filed. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy must receive relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent before they can be removed. Key value: Notice to Quit periods range from 3 days to 18 months depending on cause; relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy eviction = 6 times monthly rent. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Qualifying senior citizens (62+ before conversion recording), permanently disabled persons, or disabled veterans (60%+ service-connected disability) who have lived in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership for at least one year before the conversion recording may be protected from eviction for up to 40 years, provided their household income does not exceed the greater of three times the county average per-person income or $50,000. Key value: Up to 40 years protected tenancy; income cap = greater of 3x county average per-person income or $50,000. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord of residential rental property may not refuse to renew a tenant's lease or evict a tenant without good cause, as defined by the statute's list of permitted grounds for eviction. This protection does not apply to owner-occupied buildings of two or three units, motels, hotels, or transient or seasonal units. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a landlord evicts a tenant on the ground of wanting to personally occupy the unit, the landlord must actually occupy it for at least six months, or else owes the former tenant treble damages plus attorney fees and costs. If a landlord evicts a tenant to permanently board up, demolish, or retire a building from residential use, the landlord cannot return any unit to residential use for five years, or else owes treble damages, attorney fees/costs, and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, and the property cannot be registered as a planned real estate development during that five-year period. Key value: 6-month personal-occupancy requirement; 5-year residential-use restriction after demolition/retirement notice; civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation; treble damages plus attorney fees/costs. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 3 units or fewer). A landlord cannot evict a tenant, substantially alter the lease or its terms, or refuse to renew a lease in reprisal for the tenant exercising certain civil rights, such as enforcing lease or legal rights, making a good-faith health/safety complaint (after first notifying the landlord), or participating in a tenant organization. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. Before a tenant can be evicted due to foreclosure, the new owner who purchased the property and wants to personally occupy it as a primary residence must give the tenant a 90-day notice to quit; this notice may be given up to 90 days before an existing lease expires, and tenants with longer remaining leases cannot be evicted until the lease ends and the 90-day notice has also been given. Key value: 90-day notice to quit. [N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord must file a registration statement (with the municipal clerk for one- or two-family non-owner-occupied homes, or with the Bureau of Housing Inspection for buildings with three or more units). A landlord who has not properly registered is barred from evicting a tenant from the building. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-27; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. New Jersey has no state law that caps or controls rent, but municipalities may pass local rent control or rent-leveling ordinances. Where no local ordinance applies, a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rate, and the increase must not be unconscionable (so unreasonable as to shock the conscience). [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This prohibition applies to all tenants in the building regardless of protected-tenancy status. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

May apply: coverage depends on year built, which the data does not include. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinance for 30 years following completion of construction of the building. Key value: 30 years. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). Landlords and rental agencies may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise discriminate against, prospective tenants based on source of lawful income (such as housing vouchers or public assistance), along with race, creed, color, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, and other protected categories. [N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 4 units or fewer). NJ housing providers cannot ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record until after making a conditional offer of tenancy (except methamphetamine-manufacturing convictions on federally assisted housing and lifetime sex-offender-registry status). After a conditional offer, a provider may only consider: certain serious violent/sexual felonies (no time limit), 1st-degree indictable offenses within the prior 6 years, 2nd/3rd-degree offenses within 4 years, and 4th-degree offenses within 1 year. Arrests without conviction, expunged or pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications, and sealed records can never be considered. A conditional offer may only be withdrawn based on a qualifying record if necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, following an individualized assessment and with written notice and appeal rights to the applicant. Key value: Lookback: permanent bar for enumerated violent/sexual felonies; 6 years (1st degree); 4 years (2nd/3rd degree); 1 year (4th degree). [N.J.S.A. 46:8-56; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned, less lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear or other money owed under the lease, sent by personal delivery, registered, or certified mail along with an itemized list of any deductions. Key value: 30 days. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 3 units or fewer). A New Jersey landlord is not required to collect a security deposit, but if one is collected it cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent (combined with any pet deposit), and any yearly increase to the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit amount. Prepaid rent (including last month's rent) counts toward this cap, so total upfront charges (security deposit plus first month's rent) cannot exceed two and one-half times the monthly rent. Key value: max 1.5x monthly rent; annual increase cap 10% of current deposit. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0439.explanation: Applies. It is unlawful to use or distribute a 'common pricing algorithm' as part of an anticompetitive conspiracy to restrain trade, or to use/distribute such an algorithm to coerce another party into setting or adopting the price or commercial term it recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. [Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California landlords may charge a prospective tenant a screening/application fee only up to an annually-adjusted statutory cap; for 2026 the maximum is $68.96. The fee may only cover the cost of obtaining things like a consumer credit report and processing the application, unused portions must be refunded, and the fee cannot be charged if no unit is actually available or (unless using a first-qualified-applicant policy) to applicants not ultimately selected. Key value: $68.96 (2026 cap, adjusted annually). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is older than 15 years, not a single-family home, not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). After a tenant (or all tenants, if added later) has lawfully occupied a rental unit for 12 months (or 24 months in some multi-tenant situations), the landlord cannot end the tenancy without a legally recognized 'just cause' reason, which must be stated in the written termination notice. For no-fault terminations (e.g., owner move-in, demolition/substantial remodel, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate), the landlord must also pay the tenant one month's rent as relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent. Key value: 1 month's rent (relocation assistance/rent waiver for no-fault terminations). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. When a tenant is temporarily displaced for less than 20 days to allow capital improvement work, relocation payments are governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 rather than the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's general relocation provision; San Francisco publishes a daily relocation rate used in that context of $446.00/day plus actual moving expenses for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. Key value: $446.00/day plus actual moving expenses (3/1/26-2/28/27). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Under the State's Housing Crisis Act, only lower-income households (80% AMI or below) displaced for demolition of a unit that the owner will replace with new construction must receive relocation payments consistent with the relocation benefits required to be paid by public entities under Government Code Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 7260); other displaced tenants need only receive the local RSO/JCO minimum amounts, enhanced only if the HCA or RPO requires it. Key value: Relocation payment per public-entity relocation benefit standards (Gov. Code Ch. 16, § 7260 et seq.) for lower-income (≤80% AMI) households displaced by demolition for new construction. [Cal. Gov. Code § 66300.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Covered, but the stricter local rule governs here (Annual Allowable Rent Increase under San Francisco Rent Ordinance, S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37). An owner of residential real property cannot raise the rent on a covered unit by more than 5% plus the local change in the cost of living (CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, and can only impose up to two such increases within that 12-month period. The cap does not apply to the initial rent set for a new tenancy once prior tenants have vacated. Key value: 5% + CPI, max 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California state law requires landlords to give tenants at least 30 days' written advance notice before a rent increase that is less than 10%. Key value: 30 days' notice for increases < 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 827; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Narrow exceptions allow higher deposits for small landlords, long-term leases, and in certain service-member cases, and deposits must be itemized and returned within 21 days of move-out. Key value: 1 month's rent (up to 2 months' rent for small landlords: natural persons/LLCs of natural persons owning ≤2 rental properties totaling ≤4 units). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords in San Francisco may not sell or use algorithmic devices (software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data) to recommend what rent to charge for a vacant unit or to manage occupancy levels. Tenants or the City Attorney may sue to enforce the ban. [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.10C; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords who evict tenants by withdrawing units from the rental market under the Ellis Act must pay relocation benefits to each tenant, subject to a maximum per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant. Key value: $11,110.05 per tenant; $33,330.13 max per unit; +$7,443.90 per elderly (62+)/disabled tenant (rates for 3/1/26-2/28/27, adjusted annually). [S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord must have one of 17 enumerated "just cause" reasons as the dominant motive to evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance. The mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not by itself constitute just cause. Key value: 17 enumerated just cause reasons. [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords who withdraw units from rental housing use under the Ellis Act must pay relocation assistance to each tenant, up to a maximum per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant. Key value: $11,110.05 per tenant; $33,330.13 max per unit; +$7,443.90 for each elderly (62+)/disabled tenant (3/1/26-2/28/27). [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9A; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Covered, but the stricter local rule governs here (Relocation Payments for Temporary Displacement Under 20 Days for Capital Improvement Work, Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9). When a San Francisco landlord terminates a tenancy for owner/relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal of the unit from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation, the landlord must pay relocation assistance to each tenant, up to a maximum per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant or household with minor children. Key value: $8,245.00 per tenant; $24,733.00 max per unit; +$5,497.00 for each elderly (60+)/disabled tenant or household with minor children (3/1/26-2/28/27). [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9C; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance may raise rent only up to the annually published allowable percentage set by the Rent Board; for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 that allowable increase is 1.6%. Key value: 1.6% for 3/1/2026-2/28/2027. [S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance limits how arrest or conviction history can be used against applicants and residents in decisions about affordable housing, protecting people with a criminal record from being automatically denied or evicted from affordable housing on that basis. [S.F. Police Code art. 49; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. San Francisco landlords must pay tenants annual interest on security deposits at the rate published yearly by the Rent Board; for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 that rate is 4.2%. Key value: 4.2% annual interest for 3/1/2026-2/28/2027. [S.F. Admin. Code ch. 49; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

When an applicant has a government rent subsidy, the landlord's income-eligibility standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant personally pays, and if the landlord uses the applicant's credit history, it must let the applicant instead provide alternative proof of ability to pay (e.g., benefit records, pay stubs, bank statements) and reasonably consider that evidence. [Cal. Gov. Code § 12955; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord generally cannot demand or receive a security deposit worth more than one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent. Narrow exceptions allow higher deposits for small landlords, long-term leases, and in certain service-member cases, and deposits must be itemized and returned within 21 days of move-out. Key value: 1 month's rent (up to 2 months' rent for small landlords: natural persons/LLCs of natural persons owning ≤2 rental properties totaling ≤4 units). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords in San Francisco may not sell or use algorithmic devices (software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data) to recommend what rent to charge for a vacant unit or to manage occupancy levels. Tenants or the City Attorney may sue to enforce the ban. [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.10C; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords who evict tenants by withdrawing units from the rental market under the Ellis Act must pay relocation benefits to each tenant, subject to a maximum per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant. Key value: $11,110.05 per tenant; $33,330.13 max per unit; +$7,443.90 per elderly (62+)/disabled tenant (rates for 3/1/26-2/28/27, adjusted annually). [S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord must have one of 17 enumerated "just cause" reasons as the dominant motive to evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance. The mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not by itself constitute just cause. Key value: 17 enumerated just cause reasons. [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords who withdraw units from rental housing use under the Ellis Act must pay relocation assistance to each tenant, up to a maximum per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant. Key value: $11,110.05 per tenant; $33,330.13 max per unit; +$7,443.90 for each elderly (62+)/disabled tenant (3/1/26-2/28/27). [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9A; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Covered, but the stricter local rule governs here (Relocation Payments for Temporary Displacement Under 20 Days for Capital Improvement Work, Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9). When a San Francisco landlord terminates a tenancy for owner/relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal of the unit from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation, the landlord must pay relocation assistance to each tenant, up to a maximum per unit, plus an additional amount for each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant or household with minor children. Key value: $8,245.00 per tenant; $24,733.00 max per unit; +$5,497.00 for each elderly (60+)/disabled tenant or household with minor children (3/1/26-2/28/27). [S.F. Admin. Code § 37.9C; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance may raise rent only up to the annually published allowable percentage set by the Rent Board; for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 that allowable increase is 1.6%. Key value: 1.6% for 3/1/2026-2/28/2027. [S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance limits how arrest or conviction history can be used against applicants and residents in decisions about affordable housing, protecting people with a criminal record from being automatically denied or evicted from affordable housing on that basis. [S.F. Police Code art. 49; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. San Francisco landlords must pay tenants annual interest on security deposits at the rate published yearly by the Rent Board; for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 that rate is 4.2%. Key value: 4.2% annual interest for 3/1/2026-2/28/2027. [S.F. Admin. Code ch. 49; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

[Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California landlords may charge a prospective tenant a screening/application fee only up to an annually-adjusted statutory cap; for 2026 the maximum is $68.96. The fee may only cover the cost of obtaining things like a consumer credit report and processing the application, unused portions must be refunded, and the fee cannot be charged if no unit is actually available or (unless using a first-qualified-applicant policy) to applicants not ultimately selected. Key value: $68.96 (2026 cap, adjusted annually). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

May apply: coverage depends on year built, which the data does not include. After a tenant (or all tenants, if added later) has lawfully occupied a rental unit for 12 months (or 24 months in some multi-tenant situations), the landlord cannot end the tenancy without a legally recognized 'just cause' reason, which must be stated in the written termination notice. For no-fault terminations (e.g., owner move-in, demolition/substantial remodel, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate), the landlord must also pay the tenant one month's rent as relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent. Key value: 1 month's rent (relocation assistance/rent waiver for no-fault terminations). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. When a tenant is temporarily displaced for less than 20 days to allow capital improvement work, relocation payments are governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 rather than the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's general relocation provision; San Francisco publishes a daily relocation rate used in that context of $446.00/day plus actual moving expenses for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. Key value: $446.00/day plus actual moving expenses (3/1/26-2/28/27). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Under the State's Housing Crisis Act, only lower-income households (80% AMI or below) displaced for demolition of a unit that the owner will replace with new construction must receive relocation payments consistent with the relocation benefits required to be paid by public entities under Government Code Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 7260); other displaced tenants need only receive the local RSO/JCO minimum amounts, enhanced only if the HCA or RPO requires it. Key value: Relocation payment per public-entity relocation benefit standards (Gov. Code Ch. 16, § 7260 et seq.) for lower-income (≤80% AMI) households displaced by demolition for new construction. [Cal. Gov. Code § 66300.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

May apply: coverage depends on year built, which the data does not include. An owner of residential real property cannot raise the rent on a covered unit by more than 5% plus the local change in the cost of living (CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, and can only impose up to two such increases within that 12-month period. The cap does not apply to the initial rent set for a new tenancy once prior tenants have vacated. Key value: 5% + CPI, max 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California state law requires landlords to give tenants at least 30 days' written advance notice before a rent increase that is less than 10%. Key value: 30 days' notice for increases < 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 827; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a prospective tenant furnishes the landlord with a reusable (portable) tenant screening report, the landlord must use that report rather than requiring the applicant to pay for a new one. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord may not terminate a residential tenancy covered by this Division without just cause, which must be either an at-fault cause (e.g., nonpayment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to renew a substantially similar lease, criminal activity/threats, unauthorized sublet, refusal of entry, unlawful use, holdover employee-occupant, failure to surrender after notice) or a no-fault cause (owner/family move-in for at least 12 continuous months, withdrawal from the rental market, compliance with a government habitability/vacate order, or demolition/substantial remodel). Applies. For a no-fault just cause termination, the landlord must give written notice (30 or 60 days per Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1) describing the basis for termination and stating the tenant's right to relocation assistance. Regardless of the tenant's income or length of tenancy, the landlord must provide relocation assistance equal to two months of actual rent (three months if the tenant is a senior or disabled), paid directly or via rent waiver. If the unit is re-offered for rent within five years of a no-fault eviction under the owner-move-in, government-order, or demolition/remodel grounds, the landlord must first offer to re-lease the unit to the displaced tenant. Key value: 2 months' actual rent relocation assistance (3 months if tenant is senior or disabled); 30-60 days' written notice. [San Diego Municipal Code § 98.0706; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords evicting a tenant for an enumerated not-at-fault reason (owner/family/manager occupancy, demolition/conversion/removal from rental use, government order to vacate, HUD-ordered vacation, residential hotel conversion, conversion to affordable housing, or demolition/conversion to condos/hotels/commercial use) from a unit covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or Just Cause Ordinance (JCO) must pay relocation assistance per unit and file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD before serving the termination notice, with a copy of the notice filed with LAHD within 3 days of service. Relocation amounts (effective 7/1/2026-6/30/2027) range from $11,000 (eligible tenant, <3 years) to $27,400 (qualified tenant, 3+ years or low income), paid within 15 days of the notice, and increase every July 1. Key value: $11,000-$27,400 per unit by tenant/tenancy category (Chart A, 7/1/2026-6/30/2027), increasing every July 1; payment due within 15 days of notice. [L.A. Mun. Code § 151.09; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is built after 1978-10-01). Landlords of most residential rental units in the City of Los Angeles that are NOT regulated by the City's Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) may terminate a tenancy only for an enumerated just cause, once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired (whichever comes first). At-fault causes (no relocation assistance owed) include failure to pay rent, uncured lease violations, nuisance or property damage, illegal use of the unit, failure to renew a similar rental agreement, denying the landlord reasonable access, or an unapproved subtenant remaining after the lease ends. No-fault causes (owner/immediate-family move-in, required resident-manager move-in, demolition/permanent removal from the rental market/conversion to non-residential use, government order to vacate, HUD sale of the property, conversion/demolition of a residential hotel, or conversion to affordable housing) require the landlord to pay the tenant relocation assistance. Separately, effective March 27, 2023, a landlord in an RSO or JCO unit may not evict a tenant for unpaid rent unless the amount owed exceeds the HUD Fair Market Rent for the unit's bedroom size. Landlords must register covered units annually with LAHD, display the Registration Certificate, post a Notice of Right to Counsel (beginning August 20, 2025), and provide/post a Notice of Renters' Protections for tenancies beginning or renewing on or after January 27, 2023. All eviction notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days of service. [L.A. Municipal Code § 151.30; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. For 'Protected Units' demolished for new construction, the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict or Notice of Intent to Withdraw with LAHD, serve tenants written notice, and provide occupant protections including the right to relocation, the right to remain in the unit up to 6 months before construction begins (with 6-month move-out notice), the right to return to the unit if demolition does not proceed, a right of first refusal to the new building for some tenants, and tenant notification requirements. Lower-income households must be paid enhanced relocation (Chart B); above-low-income households receive RSO/JCO Chart A amounts. The owner must choose one of three compliance options (standardized payment, comparable replacement unit, or individualized relocation) and pay the highest amount required by State and City law. Key value: Chart B lower-income relocation (7/1/2026-6/30/2027): Extremely Low $115,480; Very Low $96,750; Low Income per Chart A ($14,400 eligible/$27,400 qualified); above-low-income per Chart A ($11,000-$27,400); penalty starting at $250,000 per displaced unit for noncompliance. [L.A. Ord. No. 188481; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is built after 1978-10-01). Landlords of covered rental units in the City of Los Angeles may only terminate a tenancy for a specific list of 'at-fault' or 'no-fault' reasons; tenants evicted for a no-fault reason (e.g., owner/family move-in, demolition, conversion to non-residential use, government order to vacate) are entitled to relocation assistance, while tenants evicted for an at-fault reason (e.g., nonpayment of rent, lease violation, nuisance) are not. Landlords must also register covered units annually, post required tenant-protection and right-to-counsel notices, and file all eviction notices with LAHD within 3 business days of service. For nonpayment-based evictions, a landlord may not evict a tenant whose unpaid rent does not exceed the applicable Fair Market Rent (FMR) for the unit's bedroom size. [Los Angeles Municipal Code ch. XV, art. 1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords of units covered by the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) may raise rent once a year by an annually-announced percentage; for the period July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026 that allowable increase is 3%. Starting February 2, 2026, landlords can no longer tack on an additional percentage increase for utilities on top of the allowable increase. Key value: 3%. [L.A. Mun. Code § 151.06; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0444.explanation: Applies. Before ending a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy, a landlord or foreclosing owner must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit or Notice of Lease Non-renewal, and must send a copy of that notice together with a Certificate of Compliance/Service to the City's Office of Housing Stability. [Boston, Mass. Ordinances § 10-11.7; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. All landlords in Boston who plan to end a tenancy must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time they serve a Notice to Quit or Notice of non-renewal, and must separately report the notice (with tenant contact info and a copy of the notice) to the City through an online portal. Failure to comply can result in a warning (first offense) or a fine of up to $300 per day (second and subsequent offenses); a violation does not halt the eviction process. Key value: $300 per day (2nd+ offense); warning for 1st offense; up to $300/day for failure to submit to city portal. [Boston, Mass., Code of Ordinances § 10-11.7; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Covered housing providers may not use a blanket policy denying housing based on arrests or convictions; applicants must be considered case-by-case. Providers may not consider arrests without conviction, convictions subject to judicial relief (expungement/sealing), juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old, unless there is a direct relationship between the conviction and the housing sought or an unreasonable risk of harm to others' safety. Key value: 5 years (conviction look-back period). [Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

As of the query date it has only been reported favorably by the Joint Committee on Housing and referred to House Ways and Means; the bill text with specific substantive restrictions is not included in this source. [MA H.5222; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

As of the document date it has only been reported favorably out of the Joint Committee on Housing and referred to Senate Ways and Means; it has not been enacted. Applies. A tenant cannot be charged a real estate broker's fee for finding a rental unless the tenant is the one who hired the broker; if the landlord or landlord's agent engaged the broker, the landlord must pay the fee. [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 112, § 87DDD1/2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. At or before the start of a tenancy, a landlord or their agent may not require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay more than: (i) the first full month's rent, (ii) the last full month's rent at the same rate as the first month, (iii) a security deposit equal to one month's rent (or, where authorized, a fee in lieu of deposit), and (iv) the cost of purchasing and installing a key and lock. No separate application or screening fee beyond these amounts may be charged. Key value: Allowed upfront charges limited to: first month's rent + last month's rent + 1 month's rent security deposit + key/lock cost; no other fees permitted. [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Before a landlord can end a tenancy for nonpayment of rent under a written lease, the landlord must give the tenant 14 days' written notice to quit. The tenant can stop the eviction by paying or tendering all rent due, plus interest and court costs, to the landlord (or the landlord's attorney) on or before the day the tenant's answer is due in the eviction case. If the tenant's nonpayment was caused by a delay in a government benefit, subsistence or rental payment (other than a salary) reaching the tenant or landlord, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days to notify the responsible agency, and if all rent, interest and costs are then paid within that time, the tenancy is treated as not terminated. Key value: 14 days' notice to quit. [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord must give a tenant at will three months' written notice to terminate the tenancy (or, if rent is paid more often than every three months, notice equal to the rental interval or 30 days, whichever is longer). For nonpayment of rent, only 14 days' written notice to quit is required, but if the tenant has not received a similar nonpayment notice in the preceding 12 months, the tenant may cure by paying the full rent due within 10 days of receiving the notice, and the notice itself must contain specific statutory language informing the tenant of this right. Key value: 14 days' notice to quit (nonpayment); 10-day cure right; 3 months' notice (at-will termination). [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. When a landlord gives a tenant a written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, the notice must be accompanied by a state-developed form disclosing any repayment agreements, information on rental assistance programs and legal protections, and a prominent statement that the notice is not an eviction and the tenant is entitled to a court proceeding before being forced to leave. Courts may not accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof this form was delivered to the tenant. [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 31; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Massachusetts cities and towns are barred from enacting or enforcing rent control. A city or town may only adopt rent control if it formally accepts this chapter, and even then compliance becomes entirely voluntary for property owners after six months, the regulation cannot apply to units owned by an entity with fewer than ten rental units or with fair market rent over $400, and the municipality must compensate owners for the gap between market and controlled rent out of its general funds. Key value: Exempts units owned by entities with <10 rental units or fair market rent >$400; after 6 months compliance is voluntary. [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40P, § 4; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord may not require a security deposit greater than the first month's rent, and the deposit must be placed in an interest-bearing bank account in Massachusetts, accompanied by a written statement of the premises' condition, and returned (with interest) within 30 days after tenancy ends, subject to itemized deductions for unpaid rent/taxes or tenant-caused damage. As of an August 1, 2025 amendment, the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities may also authorize a landlord and tenant to agree to a recurring or scheduled fee in lieu of a deposit instead, but the fee must be optional, cannot be set based on the tenant's income, race, gender, disability, immigration status, household size or credit score, and the combined total of any such fee plus any deposit actually paid cannot exceed one month's rent. Key value: 1 month's rent (deposit cap); fee-in-lieu alternative also capped at 1 month's rent combined total. [Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0445.explanation: Applies. It is unlawful to use or distribute a 'common pricing algorithm' as part of an anticompetitive conspiracy to restrain trade, or to use/distribute such an algorithm to coerce another party into setting or adopting the price or commercial term it recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. [Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California landlords may charge a prospective tenant a screening/application fee only up to an annually-adjusted statutory cap; for 2026 the maximum is $68.96. The fee may only cover the cost of obtaining things like a consumer credit report and processing the application, unused portions must be refunded, and the fee cannot be charged if no unit is actually available or (unless using a first-qualified-applicant policy) to applicants not ultimately selected. Key value: $68.96 (2026 cap, adjusted annually). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is older than 15 years, not a single-family home, not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). After a tenant (or all tenants, if added later) has lawfully occupied a rental unit for 12 months (or 24 months in some multi-tenant situations), the landlord cannot end the tenancy without a legally recognized 'just cause' reason, which must be stated in the written termination notice. For no-fault terminations (e.g., owner move-in, demolition/substantial remodel, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate), the landlord must also pay the tenant one month's rent as relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent. Key value: 1 month's rent (relocation assistance/rent waiver for no-fault terminations). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. When a tenant is temporarily displaced for less than 20 days to allow capital improvement work, relocation payments are governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 rather than the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's general relocation provision; San Francisco publishes a daily relocation rate used in that context of $446.00/day plus actual moving expenses for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. Key value: $446.00/day plus actual moving expenses (3/1/26-2/28/27). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Under the State's Housing Crisis Act, only lower-income households (80% AMI or below) displaced for demolition of a unit that the owner will replace with new construction must receive relocation payments consistent with the relocation benefits required to be paid by public entities under Government Code Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 7260); other displaced tenants need only receive the local RSO/JCO minimum amounts, enhanced only if the HCA or RPO requires it. Key value: Relocation payment per public-entity relocation benefit standards (Gov. Code Ch. 16, § 7260 et seq.) for lower-income (≤80% AMI) households displaced by demolition for new construction. [Cal. Gov. Code § 66300.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Covered, but the stricter local rule governs here (RSO Annual Allowable Rent Increase Percentage, L.A. Mun. Code § 151.06). An owner of residential real property cannot raise the rent on a covered unit by more than 5% plus the local change in the cost of living (CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, and can only impose up to two such increases within that 12-month period. The cap does not apply to the initial rent set for a new tenancy once prior tenants have vacated. Key value: 5% + CPI, max 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. California state law requires landlords to give tenants at least 30 days' written advance notice before a rent increase that is less than 10%. Key value: 30 days' notice for increases < 10%. [Cal. Civ. Code § 827; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a prospective tenant furnishes the landlord with a reusable (portable) tenant screening report, the landlord must use that report rather than requiring the applicant to pay for a new one. [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A housing provider may check an applicant's criminal history, but may not rely on arrests that did not lead to conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or juvenile justice records, and may not impose a blanket ban excluding all applicants with any criminal history. Any denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and to the health and safety of others, considering the nature/severity of the offense and time elapsed. [Cal. Code Regs. tit. 2, § 12269; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords may not use a financial or income standard for rental housing that fails to count the combined income of unmarried co-applicants the same way it would count married applicants' combined income. When an applicant has a government rent subsidy, the landlord's income-eligibility standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant personally pays, and if the landlord uses the applicant's credit history, it must let the applicant instead provide alternative proof of ability to pay (e.g., benefit records, pay stubs, bank statements) and reasonably consider that evidence. [Cal. Gov. Code § 12955; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. A landlord generally cannot demand or receive a security deposit worth more than one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent. Narrow exceptions allow higher deposits for small landlords, long-term leases, and in certain service-member cases, and deposits must be itemized and returned within 21 days of move-out. Key value: 1 month's rent (up to 2 months' rent for small landlords: natural persons/LLCs of natural persons owning ≤2 rental properties totaling ≤4 units). [Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords evicting a tenant for an enumerated not-at-fault reason (owner/family/manager occupancy, demolition/conversion/removal from rental use, government order to vacate, HUD-ordered vacation, residential hotel conversion, conversion to affordable housing, or demolition/conversion to condos/hotels/commercial use) from a unit covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or Just Cause Ordinance (JCO) must pay relocation assistance per unit and file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD before serving the termination notice, with a copy of the notice filed with LAHD within 3 days of service. Relocation amounts (effective 7/1/2026-6/30/2027) range from $11,000 (eligible tenant, <3 years) to $27,400 (qualified tenant, 3+ years or low income), paid within 15 days of the notice, and increase every July 1. Key value: $11,000-$27,400 per unit by tenant/tenancy category (Chart A, 7/1/2026-6/30/2027), increasing every July 1; payment due within 15 days of notice. [L.A. Mun. Code § 151.09; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. For 'Protected Units' demolished for new construction, the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict or Notice of Intent to Withdraw with LAHD, serve tenants written notice, and provide occupant protections including the right to relocation, the right to remain in the unit up to 6 months before construction begins (with 6-month move-out notice), the right to return to the unit if demolition does not proceed, a right of first refusal to the new building for some tenants, and tenant notification requirements. Lower-income households must be paid enhanced relocation (Chart B); above-low-income households receive RSO/JCO Chart A amounts. The owner must choose one of three compliance options (standardized payment, comparable replacement unit, or individualized relocation) and pay the highest amount required by State and City law. Key value: Chart B lower-income relocation (7/1/2026-6/30/2027): Extremely Low $115,480; Very Low $96,750; Low Income per Chart A ($14,400 eligible/$27,400 qualified); above-low-income per Chart A ($11,000-$27,400); penalty starting at $250,000 per displaced unit for noncompliance. [L.A. Ord. No. 188481; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is built before 1978-10-01, at least 2 units, not a single-family home). Landlords of RSO-covered rental units may only terminate a tenancy for an enumerated legal cause: tenant at-fault causes (nonpayment of rent, lease violation, nuisance/damage, illegal use, failure to renew a similar agreement, denial of reasonable access, unapproved subtenancy) or no-fault causes (owner/family move-in, resident manager move-in, demolition/permanent removal from the rental market, government order, conversion to affordable housing). All termination notices must be filed with LAHD within three business days of service on the tenant. No-fault evictions require a filed Landlord Declaration of Intent to Evict, a 30- or 60-day written notice (up to 120 days or a 1-year extension in some cases), and payment of tenant relocation assistance. Key value: Notice filing within 3 business days of service; no-fault notice of 30-60 days (up to 120 days or 1-year extension). [Los Angeles Mun. Code § 151.09; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Landlords of units covered by the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) may raise rent once a year by an annually-announced percentage; for the period July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026 that allowable increase is 3%. Starting February 2, 2026, landlords can no longer tack on an additional percentage increase for utilities on top of the allowable increase. Key value: 3%. [L.A. Mun. Code § 151.06; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is built before 1978-10-01, at least 2 units, not a single-family home). For properties covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance, a landlord may raise rent only once every 12 months, by an allowable rent increase percentage set by LAHD. As of February 2, 2026, landlords may no longer tack on an extra percentage increase for utilities, and the prior 10% surcharge for an added dependent is no longer permitted (a 10% increase for a non-dependent additional tenant is still allowed, chargeable within 60 days of learning of the added tenant). Landlords may also pass through fixed monthly surcharges for unit registration ($1.61, with the actual annual fee at $38.75 since 1/1/2020), 50% of the Systematic Code Enforcement Fee (since 1/1/2022), and a $3.00 smoke/carbon-monoxide detector surcharge; rent increases above the allowable percentage require LAHD approval under specific programs (capital improvements, primary renovation, seismic retrofit, rehabilitation, or a 'just and reasonable' income-based increase). Key value: 1 increase per 12-month period, by the LAHD-published allowable %; utility surcharge add-on eliminated 2/2/2026; $1.61/mo registration surcharge ($38.75 annual fee basis since 1/1/2020); $3.00 smoke detector surcharge. [Los Angeles Mun. Code § 151.00; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0446.explanation: Applies. Before ending a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy, a landlord or foreclosing owner must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit or Notice of Lease Non-renewal, and must send a copy of that notice together with a Certificate of Compliance/Service to the City's Office of Housing Stability. [Boston, Mass. Ordinances § 10-11.7; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. All landlords in Boston who plan to end a tenancy must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time they serve a Notice to Quit or Notice of non-renewal, and must separately report the notice (with tenant contact info and a copy of the notice) to the City through an online portal. Failure to comply can result in a warning (first offense) or a fine of up to $300 per day (second and subsequent offenses); a violation does not halt the eviction process. Key value: $300 per day (2nd+ offense); warning for 1st offense; up to $300/day for failure to submit to city portal. [Boston, Mass., Code of Ordinances § 10-11.7; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Covered housing providers may not use a blanket policy denying housing based on arrests or convictions; applicants must be considered case-by-case. Providers may not consider arrests without conviction, convictions subject to judicial relief (expungement/sealing), juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old, unless there is a direct relationship between the conviction and the housing sought or an unreasonable risk of harm to others' safety. Key value: 5 years (conviction look-back period). [Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0447.explanation: Applies. Landlords in Hoboken are banned from using software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor rental data (like prices, occupancy levels, and security deposits less than 365 days old) to coordinate or set rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels with other landlords. Key value: Fine up to $2,000 or up to 90 days community service. Possible conflict with another published value or date for this rule, P.L.2026, c.43: flagged for human review. [Hoboken City Code § 158-2; source retrieved 2026-10-03]

Enacted but not yet in force: takes effect 2027-07-01. Bans landlords from using, paying for, or facilitating an algorithmic 'coordinator' (software or device) that collects competitively sensitive data (prices, lease terms, security deposits, occupancy levels) from multiple rental property owners to set or recommend rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Also bans two or more rental property owners from engaging in tacit or express 'parallel pricing coordination' on rents, and makes any violation a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act. Possible conflict with Hoboken City Code § 158-2: flagged for human review. [P.L.2026, c.43; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not a single-family home). A landlord or their agent cannot charge an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental dwelling that exceeds $50. The cap is adjusted annually for inflation (CPI) and published by the Division of Consumer Affairs. Key value: $50 (adjusted annually by CPI). [N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is at least 2 units). Owners of rooming and boarding houses must follow the same good-cause and notice requirements as the general Eviction Law when evicting residents, unless the Department's Bureau of Rooming and Boarding House Standards orders otherwise. [N.J.A.C. 5:27-3.3; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord may evict a residential tenant only for one of the statutory good causes (e.g., nonpayment of rent, disorderly conduct, property damage, substantial lease violation, owner retirement of the property from residential use, conversion to condominium/cooperative, certain criminal convictions on the premises). Except for nonpayment of rent, each cause must be described in a written Notice to Quit (sometimes preceded by a Notice to Cease), with required notice periods ranging from 3 days to 18 months depending on the cause, before an eviction suit may be filed. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy must receive relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent before they can be removed. Key value: Notice to Quit periods range from 3 days to 18 months depending on cause; relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy eviction = 6 times monthly rent. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Qualifying senior citizens (62+ before conversion recording), permanently disabled persons, or disabled veterans (60%+ service-connected disability) who have lived in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership for at least one year before the conversion recording may be protected from eviction for up to 40 years, provided their household income does not exceed the greater of three times the county average per-person income or $50,000. Key value: Up to 40 years protected tenancy; income cap = greater of 3x county average per-person income or $50,000. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord of residential rental property may not refuse to renew a tenant's lease or evict a tenant without good cause, as defined by the statute's list of permitted grounds for eviction. This protection does not apply to owner-occupied buildings of two or three units, motels, hotels, or transient or seasonal units. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a landlord evicts a tenant on the ground of wanting to personally occupy the unit, the landlord must actually occupy it for at least six months, or else owes the former tenant treble damages plus attorney fees and costs. If a landlord evicts a tenant to permanently board up, demolish, or retire a building from residential use, the landlord cannot return any unit to residential use for five years, or else owes treble damages, attorney fees/costs, and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, and the property cannot be registered as a planned real estate development during that five-year period. Key value: 6-month personal-occupancy requirement; 5-year residential-use restriction after demolition/retirement notice; civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation; treble damages plus attorney fees/costs. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 3 units or fewer). A landlord cannot evict a tenant, substantially alter the lease or its terms, or refuse to renew a lease in reprisal for the tenant exercising certain civil rights, such as enforcing lease or legal rights, making a good-faith health/safety complaint (after first notifying the landlord), or participating in a tenant organization. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. Before a tenant can be evicted due to foreclosure, the new owner who purchased the property and wants to personally occupy it as a primary residence must give the tenant a 90-day notice to quit; this notice may be given up to 90 days before an existing lease expires, and tenants with longer remaining leases cannot be evicted until the lease ends and the 90-day notice has also been given. Key value: 90-day notice to quit. [N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord must file a registration statement (with the municipal clerk for one- or two-family non-owner-occupied homes, or with the Bureau of Housing Inspection for buildings with three or more units). A landlord who has not properly registered is barred from evicting a tenant from the building. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-27; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. New Jersey has no state law that caps or controls rent, but municipalities may pass local rent control or rent-leveling ordinances. Where no local ordinance applies, a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rate, and the increase must not be unconscionable (so unreasonable as to shock the conscience). [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This prohibition applies to all tenants in the building regardless of protected-tenancy status. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

May apply: coverage depends on year built, which the data does not include. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinance for 30 years following completion of construction of the building. Key value: 30 years. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). Landlords and rental agencies may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise discriminate against, prospective tenants based on source of lawful income (such as housing vouchers or public assistance), along with race, creed, color, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, and other protected categories. [N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 4 units or fewer). NJ housing providers cannot ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record until after making a conditional offer of tenancy (except methamphetamine-manufacturing convictions on federally assisted housing and lifetime sex-offender-registry status). After a conditional offer, a provider may only consider: certain serious violent/sexual felonies (no time limit), 1st-degree indictable offenses within the prior 6 years, 2nd/3rd-degree offenses within 4 years, and 4th-degree offenses within 1 year. Arrests without conviction, expunged or pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications, and sealed records can never be considered. A conditional offer may only be withdrawn based on a qualifying record if necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, following an individualized assessment and with written notice and appeal rights to the applicant. Key value: Lookback: permanent bar for enumerated violent/sexual felonies; 6 years (1st degree); 4 years (2nd/3rd degree); 1 year (4th degree). [N.J.S.A. 46:8-56; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned, less lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear or other money owed under the lease, sent by personal delivery, registered, or certified mail along with an itemized list of any deductions. Key value: 30 days. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 3 units or fewer). A New Jersey landlord is not required to collect a security deposit, but if one is collected it cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent (combined with any pet deposit), and any yearly increase to the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit amount. Prepaid rent (including last month's rent) counts toward this cap, so total upfront charges (security deposit plus first month's rent) cannot exceed two and one-half times the monthly rent. Key value: max 1.5x monthly rent; annual increase cap 10% of current deposit. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

A0448.explanation: Enacted but not yet in force: takes effect 2027-07-01. Bans landlords from using, paying for, or facilitating an algorithmic 'coordinator' (software or device) that collects competitively sensitive data (prices, lease terms, security deposits, occupancy levels) from multiple rental property owners to set or recommend rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Also bans two or more rental property owners from engaging in tacit or express 'parallel pricing coordination' on rents, and makes any violation a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act. [P.L.2026, c.43; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not a single-family home). A landlord or their agent cannot charge an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental dwelling that exceeds $50. The cap is adjusted annually for inflation (CPI) and published by the Division of Consumer Affairs. Key value: $50 (adjusted annually by CPI). [N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is at least 2 units). Owners of rooming and boarding houses must follow the same good-cause and notice requirements as the general Eviction Law when evicting residents, unless the Department's Bureau of Rooming and Boarding House Standards orders otherwise. [N.J.A.C. 5:27-3.3; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord may evict a residential tenant only for one of the statutory good causes (e.g., nonpayment of rent, disorderly conduct, property damage, substantial lease violation, owner retirement of the property from residential use, conversion to condominium/cooperative, certain criminal convictions on the premises). Except for nonpayment of rent, each cause must be described in a written Notice to Quit (sometimes preceded by a Notice to Cease), with required notice periods ranging from 3 days to 18 months depending on the cause, before an eviction suit may be filed. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy must receive relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent before they can be removed. Key value: Notice to Quit periods range from 3 days to 18 months depending on cause; relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy eviction = 6 times monthly rent. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Qualifying senior citizens (62+ before conversion recording), permanently disabled persons, or disabled veterans (60%+ service-connected disability) who have lived in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership for at least one year before the conversion recording may be protected from eviction for up to 40 years, provided their household income does not exceed the greater of three times the county average per-person income or $50,000. Key value: Up to 40 years protected tenancy; income cap = greater of 3x county average per-person income or $50,000. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.28; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord of residential rental property may not refuse to renew a tenant's lease or evict a tenant without good cause, as defined by the statute's list of permitted grounds for eviction. This protection does not apply to owner-occupied buildings of two or three units, motels, hotels, or transient or seasonal units. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a landlord evicts a tenant on the ground of wanting to personally occupy the unit, the landlord must actually occupy it for at least six months, or else owes the former tenant treble damages plus attorney fees and costs. If a landlord evicts a tenant to permanently board up, demolish, or retire a building from residential use, the landlord cannot return any unit to residential use for five years, or else owes treble damages, attorney fees/costs, and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, and the property cannot be registered as a planned real estate development during that five-year period. Key value: 6-month personal-occupancy requirement; 5-year residential-use restriction after demolition/retirement notice; civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation; treble damages plus attorney fees/costs. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 3 units or fewer). A landlord cannot evict a tenant, substantially alter the lease or its terms, or refuse to renew a lease in reprisal for the tenant exercising certain civil rights, such as enforcing lease or legal rights, making a good-faith health/safety complaint (after first notifying the landlord), or participating in a tenant organization. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. Before a tenant can be evicted due to foreclosure, the new owner who purchased the property and wants to personally occupy it as a primary residence must give the tenant a 90-day notice to quit; this notice may be given up to 90 days before an existing lease expires, and tenants with longer remaining leases cannot be evicted until the lease ends and the 90-day notice has also been given. Key value: 90-day notice to quit. [N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). A landlord must file a registration statement (with the municipal clerk for one- or two-family non-owner-occupied homes, or with the Bureau of Housing Inspection for buildings with three or more units). A landlord who has not properly registered is barred from evicting a tenant from the building. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-27; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. New Jersey has no state law that caps or controls rent, but municipalities may pass local rent control or rent-leveling ordinances. Where no local ordinance applies, a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rate, and the increase must not be unconscionable (so unreasonable as to shock the conscience). [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. If a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This prohibition applies to all tenants in the building regardless of protected-tenancy status. [N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

May apply: coverage depends on year built, which the data does not include. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinance for 30 years following completion of construction of the building. Key value: 30 years. [N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 2 units or fewer). Landlords and rental agencies may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise discriminate against, prospective tenants based on source of lawful income (such as housing vouchers or public assistance), along with race, creed, color, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, and other protected categories. [N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies (building is not an owner-occupied building of 4 units or fewer). NJ housing providers cannot ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record until after making a conditional offer of tenancy (except methamphetamine-manufacturing convictions on federally assisted housing and lifetime sex-offender-registry status). After a conditional offer, a provider may only consider: certain serious violent/sexual felonies (no time limit), 1st-degree indictable offenses within the prior 6 years, 2nd/3rd-degree offenses within 4 years, and 4th-degree offenses within 1 year. Arrests without conviction, expunged or pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications, and sealed records can never be considered. A conditional offer may only be withdrawn based on a qualifying record if necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, following an individualized assessment and with written notice and appeal rights to the applicant. Key value: Lookback: permanent bar for enumerated violent/sexual felonies; 6 years (1st degree); 4 years (2nd/3rd degree); 1 year (4th degree). [N.J.S.A. 46:8-56; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Applies. Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned, less lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear or other money owed under the lease, sent by personal delivery, registered, or certified mail along with an itemized list of any deductions. Key value: 30 days. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1; source retrieved 2026-10-01]

Key value: max 1.5x monthly rent; annual increase cap 10% of current deposit. [N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; source retrieved 2026-10-01]
